items.title: A PRC-linked crew took credentials and secrets from a renewable operator’s own code server and left its SSH keys behind
items.content_text: Acronis’ Threat Research Unit published findings on 13 September, picked up by The Hacker News on 14 September and Industrial Cyber on 15 September. It describes a campaign it attributes, with moderate confidence, to Red Heron, an actor operating in a PRC-linked context. The vehicle is CVE-2026-60004, a CVSS 9.8 remote code execution flaw in self-hosted Gitea, fixed in Gitea 1.27.1 on 27 July. Acronis says the operator began building tooling within days of the 28 July advisory and had scanned 1,386 Gitea instances across seven countries by 30 July. It confirms 11 compromised targets in five countries: Canada, the United States, Taiwan, Argentina and Sri Lanka. The Hacker News’ headline figure of 13 organisations in six countries does not match the primary report, so this page uses Acronis’ count. Two of the victims are why this leads the page. From a Taiwanese industrial-automation company the actor took repositories for a SCADA/HMI tool used in industrial control environments. It also took a surveillance and monitoring product, IoT platform integrations, a network sniffer and server configurations. At a Canadian renewable-energy operator, Acronis counts 22 separate exploitation sessions. The actor took source code, credentials and secrets, mapped the operator’s Docker networks, and planted its own SSH keys in authorized_keys for persistent access. The tooling includes an implant Acronis tracks as JITTERLY, with more than 30 post-exploitation commands, and an LD_PRELOAD Linux rootkit it calls SIXZUT. Be precise about what this is and is not. It is a confirmed compromise of an electricity-sector organisation by an actor a vendor assesses as PRC-linked. It is not a government attribution, and it is not confirmed manipulation of generation or grid control; nothing in the reporting says a plant moved. But what the actor took and left behind at the Canadian operator is what you would want if you intended to come back: credentials and secrets that authenticate to the estate, a map of how it is networked, and SSH keys that survive a password reset. No public statement says remediation is complete, and Acronis had published no new development by 24 September. One adjacent data point arrived on 21 September: GreyNoise’s report on the actor exploiting Zyxel GS1900 switches (see the advisory below) lists Gitea CVE-2026-60004 among that actor’s targets and infers, from shared command-and-control infrastructure and malware, an overlap with Red Heron. That is GreyNoise’s inference, not a confirmed link, and it changes nothing about what to do. KEV status: CISA added CVE-2026-60004 to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 25 August with a 28 August federal deadline, confirmed against the catalogue on 22 September; that deadline is long passed.

items.title: Clusters exploiting Cisco firewall management consoles include one with Sandworm-overlapping tooling and a Qilin ransomware affiliate — and Cisco’s hardening release has now shipped
items.content_text: Cisco and CISA confirmed on 9 September that CVE-2026-20079 in Cisco Secure Firewall Management Center is being exploited in the wild. It is a CVSS 10.0 authentication bypass: a remote, unauthenticated attacker sends crafted HTTP requests and gains root on the appliance. CISA added it to KEV the same day with a federal remediation deadline of 12 September, now passed. Cisco Talos describes three post-compromise clusters. UAT-12197 used CVE-2026-20079 and is not attributed to a named actor. UAT-11823 used CVE-2026-20079 together with CVE-2026-20316 and delivered Cyclops Blink malware; Talos describes “overlaps in tooling with the Sandworm APT actor”, which is not an attribution to Sandworm. UAT-11988, which Talos assesses with high confidence is a ransomware operator with TTPs consistent with Qilin affiliates, got in only through CVE-2026-20316, a CVSS 5.3 static-credential flaw that is not in KEV, then carried out reconnaissance, stole credentials and built a list of endpoints to target for encryption. On 16 September Cisco published its hardening release, cisco-sa-hardening-asaftdfmc-uvpPROhN, covering eight internally found flaws across ASA, FTD and FMC (CVE-2026-20329 to CVE-2026-20336, maximum CVSS 9.9); those eight are not reported exploited. The same day Cisco revised the FMC advisory itself to version 2.6, replacing the earlier hot fixes with security hardening releases in the 7.0.10, 7.2.12, 7.4.8, 7.6.6, 7.7.13, 10.0.2 and 10.1.0 trains, and the hardening advisory’s ASA fixed-release table was revised again on 18 September. Talos updated its post on 21 September and still describes the same three clusters. No OT impact and no utility victim has been named. But FMC is the console that configures the firewalls enforcing the boundary between your corporate network and generation, substation and DER control networks, and the tooling overlap Talos describes is with Sandworm, the actor with the longest record of causing electricity outages.

items.title: CenterPoint Energy confirms customer data was taken through an external-facing system — electric and gas delivery not affected
items.content_text: CenterPoint Energy, the Houston-based utility serving about seven million customers in Texas, Indiana, Minnesota and Ohio, said in an SEC Form 8-K filed on 14 September that an unauthorised third party obtained customer personal information through one of its external-facing systems. It found out after someone posted online claiming to hold the data. The company says electric and gas delivery has not been impacted and it does not expect a material financial effect; it has brought in outside experts and notified law enforcement and regulators. The actor claims about 7.49 million records — names, addresses, account and billing data and partial Social Security numbers — taken by abusing a public API with no rate limiting, and has leaked a 2.5 GB archive. BleepingComputer puts the intrusion window at roughly 17 August to 1 September. Neither CenterPoint nor SecurityWeek has verified the record count, and no further filing, company statement or regulator action was reported between 15 and 22 September. The actor also threatened to “attack the main infrastructure” next time; that is an unverified claim, and nothing reported links this breach to operational systems. The point for other operators is the entry route: a customer-facing API belongs to the utility’s attack surface as much as a VPN does.

items.title: A Bavarian municipal utility’s IT was encrypted and supply kept running — then it warned customers their bank details may be exposed
items.content_text: Stadtwerke Landsberg in Bavaria says attackers encrypted its central IT systems overnight into 1 September in what it calls a targeted criminal cyberattack. Its press release, posted 3 September under the heading “rebuild under way”, and reporting by The Record citing the utility say electricity, water and other essential services kept running, while phone and email contact was limited. On 7 September the utility posted a GDPR Article 34 notice to affected people saying it could not rule out access to or theft of customer data, including names, addresses, contact details and bank details. No ransomware group has claimed the attack, no extortion demand is known, and no newer statement or recovery-complete notice had appeared as of 16 September. It is the pattern that keeps recurring at smaller utilities: the business network goes down, supply holds, and the lasting damage is data exposure and recovery time — an outcome that depends on the separation between IT and operations actually holding.

items.title: Forescout finds only 13% of network segments containing OT devices hold OT alone — utilities do better than oil and gas, but not well
items.content_text: Forescout’s Vedere Labs published an analysis on 22 September of 47,700 network segments containing more than 2.5 million devices at 209 organisations. Only 13% of the segments that contain OT devices are OT-only. Nearly half mix OT with IT and IoT equipment, and UPS units, building-automation controllers and PLCs are among the devices commonly found in those mixed segments. Forescout also measures each segment’s “blast radius”, meaning how much an attacker could reach from a single foothold. It ranks oil and gas alongside business services and healthcare among the sectors with the largest averages. Utilities score lower than oil and gas, but Forescout notes that this does not make them adequately segmented. This is exposure research, not an incident. It is relevant this week because every system in the 22 September KEV batch is a way into a network, and a flat network behind it turns one compromised gateway into access to protection, SCADA and plant systems.

items.title: ENISA’s 2026 threat landscape: 4,709 hacktivist campaigns against EU states, mostly DDoS, and six in ten intrusions through known flaws
items.content_text: ENISA published its Threat Landscape 2026 report on 23 September, covering calendar year 2025. As reported by Industrial Cyber, it counts 4,709 hacktivist campaigns against EU member states, 89% of them DDoS. It attributes state-nexus activity to Russia-linked actors in 47.6% of cases, China-linked in 15.5%, North Korea-linked in 14.1% and Iran-linked in 9%. More than 48,000 new vulnerabilities were published, up 22%, and known vulnerabilities were the route in for 60% of unauthorised-access incidents. Public administration was the most-targeted sector at 31.8%. The coverage reviewed for this edition gives no energy-sector breakdown, so this page does not quote one. For European generators and transmission operators the most useful figures are two: the most common way in is still a known, patchable flaw, and the largest state-nexus share belongs to Russia-linked actors, the nexus behind the Ukrainian grid attacks of 2015 and 2016.

items.title: INL’s TOPGEAR maps who actually holds influence over a grid asset — the non-cyber vector sitting next to DOE’s provenance RFI
items.content_text: Idaho National Laboratory described on 21 September a platform it calls TOPGEAR — Technology, Organization and Person of Interest Graph Extraction, Analysis and Reporting — that builds a graph of relationships among organisations, people and infrastructure assets from public records such as SEC filings and EIA data. The stated purpose is to trace an influence path from a foreign investment, an acquisition or a board appointment through the corporate layers to a specific physical asset, so that an analyst can see who could direct decisions about a plant, a substation or its suppliers without any cyber intrusion at all. INL says the work began under its own laboratory-directed research funding with support from DOE’s Office of Cybersecurity, Energy Security and Emergency Response, the DOE Office of Electricity and DHS, was developed with the Naval Postgraduate School, and is already used by state energy offices. The capability claims are INL’s own and no independent evaluation has been published. The reason it earns a card is the company it keeps. DOE’s bulk-power-system supply-chain request for information, with comments due 9 October (see below), asks what grid-equipment provenance should mean; TOPGEAR is an attempt to answer the parallel question of ownership provenance for the operator and its suppliers. For a transmission owner the practical use is not the tool itself, which is not available for download, but the question it frames: for each critical supplier and each jointly owned facility, can you say today who could exert control, and would you find out if that changed?

items.title: August set a global ransomware record at 997 attacks, with utilities among the categories driving the rise
items.content_text: Comparitech data reported on 14 September recorded 997 ransomware attacks worldwide in August 2026 — an average of 32 a day, a 23 percent increase on July’s 809, and above the previous monthly record of 988. The reporting singles out utility, healthcare and business-services attacks as the categories behind the surge. Treat the absolute number with the usual caution — counts of this kind depend on leak-site claims and disclosure practice as much as on actual incident volume, and claimed victims are not confirmed victims. The direction of travel, however, is consistent with what operators are seeing, and the sector detail is worth more than the headline. Utility victims doubled from five in July to ten in August, the sharpest proportional rise of any category, while Qilin alone accounted for 157 claims, roughly a quarter of the month. The named utility victims in the same tracking fit that shape: the Italian water utility Alto Calore Servizi, listed by the Titan group, and Grayson Rural Electric Cooperative, listed by Qilin on 2 September with claims of service disruption and data theft. Both are leak-site claims rather than victim confirmations, and neither organisation nor CISA has acknowledged them. Qilin has made a habit of small US electric cooperatives, having claimed two Texas co-ops in late 2025, which points at the real pattern — distribution utilities without a 24-hour security operation rather than investor-owned utilities with mature monitoring. The operational lesson from this year's utility incidents is consistent: the encryption lands on the business side, and the outage — billing, dispatch support, work management, customer service — follows from IT dependence rather than from anything touching a relay.

items.title: Cyber-informed engineering argues the useful question is not how to keep attackers out, but which consequences you can design away
items.content_text: An analysis published 15 September sets out the case for cyber-informed engineering in critical infrastructure: that industrial systems operate under a constraint IT does not share, because a compromised network does not automatically have to become a catastrophic physical event. The argument is to move the security question upstream into design — identifying the physical consequences that actually matter, then engineering them out with controls that do not depend on the digital system remaining trustworthy. For the power sector this is familiar ground — the idea grew out of national-lab work on grid consequence — but the argument has sharpened: design decisions, not detection tooling, determine whether a compromised network becomes a physical event. Protection schemes, interlocks and non-digital trip paths are security controls. This is practitioner analysis rather than incident reporting; it names no victim and describes no attack, but it is the most useful lens available for operators whose detection budget will never match their consequence exposure.

items.title: Exposed PLCs and flat remote access at small US electric utilities draw fresh vendor attention
items.content_text: Reporting on 15 September covered a vendor push specifically aimed at the exposed-PLC and remote-access problem facing small US water and electric utilities — the gap that has driven federal warnings all summer. Small municipal and cooperative electric utilities carry the same exposed-controller and flat-remote-access problem that the summer’s water-sector attacks exploited, without the staff to fix it. The underlying facts are the ones that matter and they are already federally documented: the FBI and EPA warned on 30 July that actors were reaching internet-facing Rockwell Automation MicroLogix 1100 and 1400 PLCs at water and wastewater utilities, changing IP addresses and passwords, and causing loss of view and in some cases loss of control, with reported effects including pressure loss and flooding. A subsequent internet-wide scan reported by CyberScoop found roughly 4,400 exposed programmable logic controllers still reachable, including 22 in cities that had recently been attacked. Vendor marketing aside, the exposure is real, measured and unresolved.

items.title: DOE and Sandia put a language model on the least glamorous part of grid detection: preparing the data
items.content_text: The Department of Energy’s Office of Cybersecurity, Energy Security and Emergency Response and Sandia National Laboratories reported on 8 September on C2E2, a tool developed under the AI-FORTS programme that uses large language models to automate the data-engineering step in cyber-physical threat detection for the electric grid. The point is not that a model spots the attack. It is that turning heterogeneous SCADA, relay, PMU and network telemetry into a form a detection model can consume normally takes a specialist roughly two months per deployment; Sandia reports cutting that to hours, with around 95% accuracy in detecting and localising simulated threats in testing. That matters for utilities because data preparation, not algorithm choice, is what has stalled most anomaly-detection projects at the pilot stage. Sandia is clear this has not yet been trialled at an operating utility, and the next phase specifically targets hallucination-driven false or missed detections — a failure mode a control room cannot tolerate.

items.title: Eighteen frontier models were run at a real enterprise network — one completed the whole kill chain unaided
items.content_text: Booz Allen published its Cyber Weapon Index and an accompanying report on 4 September, grading eighteen frontier AI models on how much of an intrusion they can carry out without a human driving. The models were run against a representative enterprise network rather than a benchmark; the top performer completed the full sequence — reconnaissance, initial access, lateral movement and objective — unaided, while most managed individual stages. The authors’ conclusion is about time rather than novelty: nothing in the tested behaviour was a new technique, but the interval between a foothold and a consequence compresses when the attacker never pauses to think. Booz Allen also reports that defensive playbooks written specifically against autonomous attackers cut their success rate by more than 95% in the same tests. For a utility the honest question is what your detection-to-containment interval actually is between the corporate boundary and the control centre, and whether it survives an adversary working at machine pace overnight.

items.title: GRIDLOCK: modelling puts a 92% chance of a major attack on UK battery storage by 2031 — and 29% of the fleet is enough
items.content_text: Centrii published its GRIDLOCK report on 3 September, modelling what happens when an adversary uses grid-connected battery storage as the weapon rather than the target. In the scenario, compromised BESS units are commanded to swing output in concert, manipulating physical power flows to destabilise system frequency rather than saturating a network link — the report frames it as a grid-scale denial of service delivered in energy. Across 10,000 Monte Carlo runs against three security postures, Centrii puts the probability of a major attack on UK battery storage by 2031 at 92%, and calculates that compromising roughly 29% of national capacity — on the order of 400 units — could be enough to trigger a nationwide outage affecting 67 million people, with costs modelled up to £10 billion. Mandatory certification and regular attack-readiness drills cut that probability to 61% and push the earliest likely window from 2027 to 2028. A parallel run on Texas returns the same 92% figure by 2031, with economic damage modelled up to $65 billion. This is modelling rather than a reported incident, and its value is in the premise it tests: a large amount of fast-acting capacity dispatched from a small number of control planes.

items.title: Arista’s VeloCloud SD-WAN orchestrator has a CVSS 10 flaw under active exploitation — the console that configures the links to your remote sites
items.content_text: Arista published Security Advisory 0183 on 22 September for CVE-2026-93952, an improper input validation flaw (CWE-20) in on-premises VeloCloud Orchestrator (VCO), rated CVSS v3.1 10.0 and v4.0 9.5. Arista says the issue “was discovered externally and is known to be actively exploited.” It is exposed only where certificate-based authentication from VeloCloud Edges to the orchestrator is configured. The attacker needs network access to the VCO web interface and the public portion of the Edge authentication certificate, but no VCO tenant or operator credentials. Affected on-premises releases are 5.2.3.15 and earlier, 6.1.3.7 and earlier, 6.4.2.7 and earlier, and 7.0.0.2 and earlier. Fixes exist for the 5.2.3 train (5.2.3.16) and the 6.4.2 train (6.4.2.8). Arista says fixes for other supported trains are pending, so the 6.1.x and 7.0.x lines have none yet. CISA added the CVE to KEV on 22 September with a 25 September federal deadline. No victims have been named. Utilities that use VeloCloud SD-WAN to connect substations, generation sites or field offices should treat the orchestrator as a critical asset: it pushes configuration to every Edge, so control of it is control of the WAN paths into those sites.

items.title: CISA’s 22 September KEV batch is all perimeter and management gear on a three-day clock — including an F5 BIG-IP APM zero-day
items.content_text: CISA added four actively exploited vulnerabilities to the KEV catalogue on 22 September, all with a federal remediation deadline of 25 September. Three have their own cards on this page: the Check Point VPN flaw CVE-2026-85102, the Check Point management-server flaw CVE-2026-93616 and the Arista VeloCloud Orchestrator flaw CVE-2026-93952. The fourth is CVE-2026-94127 in F5 BIG-IP Access Policy Manager, a CVSS 9.8 heap-based buffer overflow that allows unauthenticated remote code execution (F5 advisory K000162605). It is exposed only where a virtual server carries both an APM access policy and an OAuth profile, so that APM acts as an OAuth authorization server. F5 has shipped engineering hotfixes for the 21.1.0, 17.5.x and 17.1.x lines. Rapid7 reported on 22 September that no public proof-of-concept had been confirmed. Attacker, victim count and start date have not been disclosed. No utility victim is named for any of the four. For a power company the pattern matters more than any single item. Every one of these systems sits on the path between the internet or corporate network and the systems that reach generation and substation control. The gap between fix and exploitation was a matter of days, and for the Check Point management flaw the exploitation came first.

items.title: A CVSS 9.8 flaw in lwIP’s MQTT client may sit inside field devices from many vendors — the work is asking suppliers, not patching a product
items.content_text: CISA published two advisories on 22 September for lwIP, the open-source lightweight TCP/IP stack embedded in a wide range of microcontroller-based devices. ICSA-26-265-01 covers CVE-2026-87121, an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787) in lwIP’s MQTT client application, rated CVSS 9.8. CISA says successful exploitation “could allow an attacker to gain full code execution on the device.” ICSA-26-265-02 covers a separate lwIP flaw where exploitation “could result in a system crash, a DoS, or memory corruption, which could lead to code execution.” Neither is reported exploited and neither is in KEV. The difficulty for asset owners is that lwIP is a library, not a product. It can sit inside controllers, IO modules, gateways, meters and sensors from many manufacturers, and only devices whose firmware uses the MQTT client are exposed to the first flaw. No list of affected device vendors had been published in the coverage reviewed for this edition. In the power sector, look first at DER, telemetry and IIoT integrations that use MQTT.

items.title: CISA’s 22 September batch carries Siemens fixes for “Copy Fail” in Linux-based SIMATIC and SIPLUS products
items.content_text: CISA published nine ICS advisories on 22 September: two for lwIP (see the lwIP card), six for Siemens and one for OpenPLC. For electricity operators the Siemens item to route first is ICSA-26-265-04, Siemens SIPLUS and SIMATIC products. CISA summarises it as: “Multiple Siemens products are vulnerable to the ‘Copy Fail’ vulnerability,” a third-party flaw in the Linux kernel those products run on. Siemens says it has released new versions for several of the affected products, so check whether yours is among them. SIPLUS is Siemens’ ruggedised line for harsh and outdoor environments, so the practical question is which of your enclosures hold one. Three more Siemens items are in the batch. ICSA-26-265-08 covers WTV676 and WTV776, where a denial-of-service flaw could force the devices into a protection mode that disables remote connectivity. ICSA-26-265-05 covers the Desigo CC building-management family, where a malicious graphics document can lead to code execution on the client. ICSA-26-265-03 covers Siveillance Control, the physical-security management platform, where an arbitrary file upload in Open Interface Services can give root on the server. Desigo CC and Siveillance matter where they run control-centre buildings or substation access control. None of the nine is reported exploited or listed in KEV.

items.title: CISA adds a Zyxel GS1900 switch flaw to KEV after GreyNoise counts 996 exploited switches in 48 countries — most on factory-default credentials
items.content_text: On 21 September CISA added CVE-2026-7273 to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue with a federal remediation deadline of 24 September. It is a stack-based buffer overflow in the CGI program of Zyxel’s GS1900-series managed switches (GS1900-8, 8HP, 10HP, 16, 24, 24E, 24EP, 24HPv2, 48 and 48HPv2) that lets an unauthenticated attacker on the LAN execute operating-system commands with a crafted HTTP request. Zyxel fixed it on 16 June in firmware 2.90(AAHH.2)C0 and the per-model equivalents, and gives no CVSS score, so none is quoted here. The KEV entry is the consequence of a GreyNoise report published the same day. GreyNoise says a single actor, active since 7 May and assessed as a Chinese speaker, exploited 996 GS1900 switches across 48 countries — Italy 133, the United States 129, Taiwan 123, France 90, South Korea 69, the Netherlands 66 — using an obfuscated Python tool that pulled running configurations and root-level hashed credentials off each switch over TFTP. Of the 996, 564 were still on factory-default credentials. The same actor exploited two WordPress flaws to take at least 18,566 records, including plaintext passwords and law-enforcement and government personal data, from an unnamed western government organisation on 22 July, and also worked through UniFi OS, Gitea CVE-2026-60004, Proxmox VE and PAN-OS GlobalProtect targets. GreyNoise infers an overlap with Red Heron from shared command-and-control and malware; that is an inference, not an observation. Hong Kong’s HKCERT made the wider point in a 15 September advisory: edge devices — VPNs, firewalls, routers, remote-access gear — remain the primary intrusion gateway, and patching alone does not remove credentials already stolen from them. For a utility the GS1900 is not a control-centre switch. It is the inexpensive managed switch that turns up in small substations, renewable-site control cabins, depots and building networks, usually installed by an integrator and never re-baselined. “LAN-based” means the exposure is management-plane reachability, and the default-credential finding says what the real control gap is.

items.title: One crafted network message can stop an ABB Freelance DCS controller
items.content_text: ABB published advisory 7PAA010706 on 18 September for CVE-2023-5778, a flaw reserved in 2023 and published only now. It is an improper handling of a length-parameter inconsistency: a specially crafted message sent to the controller makes it stop, and the attacker needs no credentials, only network reach to the controller. ABB’s machine-readable advisory rates it CVSS v3.1 7.5. Affected are Freelance DCP, AC 700F, AC 800F and AC 900F controllers on Freelance 2013 and earlier, 2013 SP1, 2016, 2016 SP1, 2019 and 2019 SP1. The fixes already ship in existing update rollups — 2013 SP1 RU06 or later, 2016 SP1 RU07 or later, 2019 SP1 RU03 or later and 2019 SP1 FP1 — and Freelance 2024 is not affected. ABB reports no exploitation and no prior public disclosure. Editorial assessment: Freelance is ABB’s process DCS, and where it runs a generating station’s auxiliary or balance-of-plant systems, a stop-the-controller condition reachable from the control network is exactly the kind of flaw that matters. Many sites run long-lived releases that never took the later rollups, so being on a supported version is not the same as being fixed.

items.title: CISA adds three exploited Linux kernel flaws to KEV — the kernel inside a lot of substation and plant edge gear
items.content_text: On 18 September CISA added three Linux kernel vulnerabilities to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue, with a federal remediation deadline of 21 September — three days, and that date has now passed with no exploitation detail published since the listing. CVE-2025-39682 is a zero-length record handling flaw in the kernel TLS receive path; CVE-2026-53266 is an out-of-bounds write in the ebtables SNAT target on systems with bridge netfilter rules; CVE-2025-39964 is a race condition in the AF_ALG crypto socket interface. This page carries no CVSS for them because the figures quoted by outlets range widely and do not match the vendor scores. Do not conflate them with the four other kernel flaws for which a researcher published local-root exploits on 18 September; those are proof-of-concept only and are not in KEV. These are local, post-access flaws — the step that turns a foothold on a Linux host into root — not remote entry points. No detail has been published on who is exploiting them or against what, and no OT vendor, product or sector has been named. None of the CVEs from CISA’s 17 September ICS advisories is among them. Editorial assessment: Linux runs historians, jump hosts, SCADA front-end servers, substation gateways and much industrial edge hardware, and vendor firmware typically trails upstream kernel fixes by months.

items.title: Rockwell extends its lock-out recovery guidance to Micro820 and Micro850 — the fifth revision since attackers began setting passwords on exposed PLCs
items.content_text: On 18 September Rockwell Automation issued revision 5.0 of SD1790, the notice it first published on 30 July under the title “Important Hardening Guidance and Instructions for Restoring Access When the Password Is Unknown”. The revision extends the recovery and hardening instructions, until now written for MicroLogix 1100 and 1400, to the Micro820 and Micro850 controllers. The premise has not changed: the notice references the FBI public service announcement of 30 July describing attackers remotely altering the configuration of internet-exposed PLCs, changing IP addresses and setting passwords where none existed, so that operators were locked out of their own controllers. There is no CVE, because there is no vulnerability — the devices did what an unauthenticated network peer told them to. Rockwell’s guidance is the familiar list: remove the controller from internet exposure, put remote access behind a VPN and firewall, set strong passwords, keep offline backups, disable the embedded HTTP server and keep firmware current. Revision 5.0 adds no new incident data. Rockwell published no new security advisories between 10 and 22 September; its last batch, SD1792 to SD1800, was 1 September. Why it is on a transmission and generation page: Micro800 and MicroLogix controllers are exactly what runs a small hydro station, a remote pump house, a switchyard auxiliary system or a co-operative’s distribution substation, often installed with a cellular modem and no firewall. The exposed-PLC finding from the FBI notice and the small-utility exposure work reported on 15 September describe the same population.

items.title: Twenty-two flaws in Pepperl+Fuchs IO-Link masters, two at CVSS 9.8 — and the same firmware ships under Phoenix Contact and Carlo Gavazzi badges
items.content_text: CERT@VDE published VDE-2026-014 on 16 September: Pepperl+Fuchs has fixed 22 vulnerabilities in the firmware of its ICE2-8IOL and ICE3-8IOL IO-Link master modules, found by Nozomi Networks researchers. Firmware before 1.7.4 is affected and the fix is 1.7.8. The two worst are CVE-2026-27546, an authentication bypass rated CVSS 9.8, and CVE-2026-27565, an unauthenticated upload of a crafted IODD device-description file that executes shell scripts, also 9.8. Between them, CVE-2026-27547 through CVE-2026-27564 are command-injection, file-inclusion and authorisation flaws rated 7.2 to 8.8 that reach root-level code execution; CVE-2026-27557, rated 7.5, is an unauthenticated path traversal that reads the module’s SSH server private keys; and CVE-2026-27553, rated 6.5, discloses password hashes. The same firmware is sold rebadged, so the advisory reaches further than the Pepperl+Fuchs name: Phoenix Contact IOL MA8 PN DI8 and IOL MA8 EIP DI8 under VDE-2026-027 (20 CVEs, same fix 1.7.8, same date) and Carlo Gavazzi YL212 and YN115 masters under VDE-2026-028. No exploitation has been reported, and no CISA advisory had appeared by 22 September. IO-Link masters sit at the sensor and actuator layer of discrete automation. In a generation estate that means balance-of-plant, fuel and water handling, coal and biomass conveying and packaged skids — the systems an OEM or panel builder specified and nobody in the control-room team has a drawing for. A device that hands out root and its own SSH keys to anyone on the PROFINET or EtherNet/IP segment is a lateral-movement foothold on the network your controllers use, which is why it belongs here despite the sector label.

items.title: ABB closed a password-reset takeover in its dynovaPRO energy-asset cloud — after spotting suspicious resets at nine customers
items.content_text: ABB published advisory 4JDE002044 on 17 September for CVE-2026-18963, rated CVSS v3.1 9.1, in dynovaPRO, ABB’s cloud system for managing energy assets such as EV chargers, batteries and photovoltaic systems. The flaw sits in the Keycloak authentication component built into the platform: an unauthenticated attacker could force the password-reset flow for any user without clicking the email verification link, which amounts to account takeover. ABB fixed it on its own side on 27 August, so customers have nothing to install, and it disabled password reset for all customers as an interim measure. ABB says the CVE was publicly disclosed on 17 August, roughly ten days before the cloud fix. ABB says it had not received confirmed reports of active exploitation as of 27 August, but its own analysis found 26 password-change events across nine customers that it treats as possible testing or reconnaissance, and it disabled those accounts. That is suspicious activity observed by the vendor, not confirmed exploitation. Editorial assessment: an account on a platform like this can change how chargers, batteries and PV behave at a site, so a takeover is a control-plane question for DER and storage owners, not only a data-exposure one.

items.title: A CVSS 10 authentication bypass in Cisco ISE is being exploited — and ISE is what decides who gets onto your OT network
items.content_text: Cisco published advisory cisco-sa-ISE-ABP-VNSW7Tn5 on 16 September for CVE-2026-76460, a CVSS 10.0 flaw in Identity Services Engine and ISE-PIC: an API endpoint with insufficient authentication lets a remote, unauthenticated attacker bypass the web-based management interface. Cisco’s PSIRT states it is aware of active exploitation. ISE 3.1 through 3.5 and ISE-PIC are affected, and ISE 3.0 and earlier are end-of-life and must be migrated; the fixed releases are 3.1 Patch 12, 3.2 Patch 11, 3.3 Patch 12, 3.4 Patch 7 and 3.5 Patch 4. CISA added the CVE to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 16 September with a federal remediation deadline of 19 September — three days, which is as short as that clock gets. That deadline has now passed. As of 22 September the Cisco advisory was still at its first revision with the exploitation statement unchanged, and Singapore’s CSA added its own alert, AL-2026-126, on 21 September. There are no workarounds; short of patching, Cisco’s only mitigation is restricting management traffic with infrastructure ACLs. No actor attribution and no exposure counts have been published. Cisco’s hunting guidance is narrow but specific: run show logging application ise-kong/access.log | include dummyuser from the admin CLI and review the API gateway access log in support bundles for the same marker. No targeting of industrial or critical-infrastructure operators has been claimed. The reason it belongs on this page is structural rather than sectoral: in most utilities ISE is the NAC and 802.1X policy engine that authorises switch ports, issues certificates and gates the remote-access paths into the industrial DMZ. Administrative control of that policy engine is administrative control of who is permitted to be on the control network, and a quiet policy change there will not look like an attack in anyone’s console.

items.title: A crafted email is enough to run commands as root on Cisco’s Secure Email Gateway
items.content_text: CVE-2026-76461 is a SQL-injection flaw in the AsyncOS email-parsing path of the Cisco Secure Email Gateway, rated CVSS 9.8. An unauthenticated attacker who sends a message carrying malicious SQL statements can reach arbitrary command execution with root privileges, with no user interaction. Cisco published advisory cisco-sa-esa-inj-2bLVGmhX on 14 September and says its PSIRT became aware of active exploitation during September; CISA added the CVE to the KEV catalogue the same day, 14 September, with a federal remediation deadline of 17 September. Both physical and virtual appliances are affected regardless of configuration, and Shadowserver counted more than 400 appliances exposed to the internet. Cisco names 16.5.0-780 as the preferred fixed release alongside fixed builds in the 15.5 and 16.0 lines; take the exact build strings from the Cisco advisory, because the outlets covering this disagree on them. Researchers quoted by Cybersecurity Dive note that on-premises gateways carry more pivot risk than cloud-hosted instances and that the flaw would suit a state-linked espionage operation. No critical-infrastructure targeting has been claimed and no attribution has been published. For a utility this is an initial-access item rather than an OT one: the mail gateway is a permanently internet-facing appliance inside the corporate estate that talks to directory services, and root on it is a well-worn first step towards the engineering network.

items.title: CISA’s 17 September batch reaches a transmission FACTS controller and an industrial edge platform
items.content_text: CISA’s Thursday 17 September release ran to eight items: seven new advisories, ICSA-26-260-01 through -07, plus one update. The new advisories cover Bransys ELD, Mitsubishi Electric GX Works3 and Motion Control Settings, Hitachi Energy’s FACTS Control Platform, Schneider Electric’s Modicon M340 controller and communication modules, Schneider Electric NetBotz 5 (models 750 and 755), ABB Ability Edgenius and Schneider Electric PowerChute Serial Shutdown. The one that matters most to this audience is Hitachi Energy’s FACTS Control Platform, which controls transmission-level flexible AC transmission equipment. Per reporting on the Hitachi Energy advisory, the platform is exposed through its embedded GWS component and inherits five 2024 CVEs first disclosed for MicroSCADA/MACH GWS: CVE-2024-4872 and CVE-2024-3980, both rated CVSS 9.9; CVE-2024-7940, rated 8.3, a service exposed on all interfaces without authentication and the one to lead with for network exposure; CVE-2024-3982, rated 8.2; and CVE-2024-7941, rated 4.3. Affected are FACTS Control Platform versions 3.4.0 through 4.1.1 where the GWS component is installed. Outlets disagree on whether a fixed release exists, so take remediation from Hitachi Energy advisory 8DBD000229 rather than assuming a patch. ABB Ability Edgenius 3.2.0.0 to 3.2.4.0, an industrial edge platform found in utility and process environments, is affected by the Linux kernel “Copy Fail” flaw CVE-2026-31431 (CVSS 7.8), fixed in 3.2.4.1. The Modicon M340 advisory is a CISA republication of a 2025 Schneider advisory: CVE-2025-6625, a denial of service via crafted FTP commands rated 7.5 under CVSS v3.1 and 8.7 under v4.0, fixed in firmware SV3.70. NetBotz 5 carries CVE-2026-13336 (6.4 under v3.1, 7.3 under v4.0) and CVE-2026-13337, fixed in 5.6.0; PowerChute Serial Shutdown carries CVE-2026-13348 (5.3 under v3.1, 6.9 under v4.0), an excessive-authentication-attempts flaw, with version 1.6 as the fix. The Mitsubishi advisory covers CVE-2026-15688, an authentication-algorithm flaw rated 8.8 under CVSS v3.1 and 8.7 under v4.0, affecting all versions and described as permitting local authentication bypass and tampering with control programs. The Bransys ELD advisory covers three hardcoded or cleartext credential issues, the highest rated 7.5, fixed in Android 11.00.00 and iOS 1.1.54. CISA reports no exploitation for anything in the batch. Separately, ICSA-26-211-07 on Mitsubishi’s CC-Link IE TSN communication protocol was updated on 17 September, adding eight affected products and removing three.

items.title: Secure Lock credentials on Schneider’s SCADAPack x70 RTUs are not protected well enough
items.content_text: CISA advisory ICSA-26-258-04, published 15 September and republishing Schneider Electric’s SEVD-2026-251-03 of 8 September, covers CVE-2026-81861 — insufficiently protected credentials in the Secure Lock feature of the SCADAPack x70 range, rated CVSS v3 6.5 and 5.9 under CVSS v4. The listed products are the SCADAPack 47x, 47xi, 47xd, 470R and 57x, with the product tree also naming the SCADAPack 3xx and 32. The consequence is unauthorised access to RTU configuration. Schneider lists no firmware fix in the advisory; the published remedy is configuration work — enable role-based access control as described in the SCADAPack security guidelines, segment the network, and use the RTU Firewall Service to restrict which services answer. No exploitation is reported. On a power system these are the RTUs behind distribution automation, recloser and capacitor-bank control, and remote telemetry, and they usually live at unmanned sites reached over a cellular or radio link. That is precisely the population that ends up outside the segmentation an operator believes is in place, which is what turns a medium-severity configuration flaw into an access-path problem.

items.title: GitLab CVSS 10 path traversal is being exploited, and grid and generation teams host more of it than they think
items.content_text: GitLab patched CVE-2026-85706 on 10 September, a path-traversal flaw in the repository commits API that it rated CVSS 10.0 and that allows an unauthenticated attacker to read arbitrary files from a GitLab server. CISA added it to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on Friday 11 September with a remediation deadline for federal agencies of Monday 14 September. watchTowr reported it was already seeing in-the-wild probes for vulnerable servers, and Hong Kong’s CERT issued its own advisory on 14 September stating the flaw is being exploited in the wild. A second flaw fixed in the same release, CVE-2026-87719, can expose sensitive information from Enterprise Edition servers. For a utility this is not a developer problem. Self-hosted GitLab is where many transmission and generation operators keep substation automation configs, EMS/SCADA integration scripts, relay setting files, DER management code and the credentials that tie them together. Unauthenticated file reads against that server hand an attacker the engineering keys to a CIP-scoped estate without ever touching a relay.

items.title: Nozomi finishes its SCALANCE LPE9403 work: twelve flaws, several chainable to root on an OT edge device
items.content_text: Two dates on this item have been reported loosely elsewhere, so take them first. Nozomi Networks Labs’ PROFINET DCP research — four memory-corruption flaws in the Siemens SCALANCE LPE9403, tracked as CVE-2025-40575 through CVE-2025-40578 and each rated CVSS 5.3 for denial of service — was published on 10 September, and those CVEs were originally disclosed in May 2025 under ICSA-25-135-18. What happened on 15 September was CISA updating that advisory to version 4 to add the SINEMA Remote Connect Edge Client and the vendor fixes; it was not a new critical advisory. On 18 September Nozomi published the second part of the research, and that is the part worth acting on. It describes twelve vulnerabilities in total — nine in the device firmware and three in the SINEMA Remote Connect Edge Client — reported with CVSS scores ranging from 5.3 to 8.5. Affected are LPE9403 firmware below V4.0 HF0 and the Edge Client up to and including V2.1; both are fixed in V4.0 HF0 and later, and Siemens has published an advisory and patches. Nozomi says several of the flaws can be chained to obtain root-level control of the device, which would allow manipulation of telemetry, suppression of alarms, access to operational data, disruption of OT services and lateral movement onto adjacent networks. There is no evidence of exploitation in the wild. In a substation or generation estate the LPE9403 is the box between the process bus and everything above it, aggregating data for EMS, historians or cloud analytics — so root on it means the numbers your control room trusts can be edited before they arrive, which is a harder problem to notice than the device going offline.

items.title: Siemens patches an authentication bypass in Reyrolle 7SR5 protection relays, the gear that trips your feeders
items.content_text: Siemens ProductCERT published SSA-142885 on 8 September, covering fourteen vulnerabilities in the Reyrolle 7SR5 protection and control relay family across every firmware version before V2.70. The lead flaw, CVE-2026-62645 at CVSS 9.8, is an information disclosure in the device web interface that lets an unauthenticated attacker calculate current and previous session identifiers and step straight past authentication. Two companion issues make that worse: weak session-token entropy in CVE-2026-62646, and a role-based access control bypass in CVE-2026-62650 that hands an attacker administrative rights. A pre-authentication denial-of-service condition is also fixed. Siemens reports no exploitation, and no change of state was found when the advisory was re-checked on 11 September. This remains the highest-consequence unexploited item on the board for transmission and distribution operators because of placement rather than score — 7SR5 relays sit in feeder, transformer and busbar protection schemes, and Siemens took the unusual step of reminding TSOs and DSOs to confirm their redundant secondary protection is healthy. Update, 15 September: CISA republished the advisory as ICSA-26-258-05, listing CVE-2026-62645 as missing authentication for a critical function and again reporting no known public exploitation. The same CISA release updated its Siemens SICAM 8 advisory (ICSA-26-197-05, fixes in V26.20) and its Siemens products-using-OpenSSL advisory (ICSA-26-174-03, CVE-2025-15467), and republished Schneider Electric’s SCADAPack x70 credential-protection flaw CVE-2026-81861 as ICSA-26-258-04.

items.content_text: CISA published ICSA-26-258-03 on 15 September for mySCADA myPRO Manager version 2.1 and earlier. items.title: “MikroTrick” moves from disclosed to confirmed exploited — two CVSS 9.2 SSH flaws hand over RouterOS admin
items.content_text: CERT Polska issued an alert on 9 September confirming that the MikroTik RouterOS vulnerability chain known as “MikroTrick” — disclosed earlier but not previously confirmed as exploited — is now being used in real-world attacks observed since at least 2 September. The chain pairs an SSH authentication bypass, CVE-2026-67276 at CVSS 9.2, with an SSH privilege-escalation flaw, CVE-2026-86060 at CVSS 9.2, to take full unauthenticated administrative control of an internet-exposed RouterOS device. A third bug, CVE-2026-67277, allows memory disclosure or denial of service through the bandwidth-test service. CERT Polska named no victims and no sectors; it noted only that MikroTik devices are widely deployed by ISPs, data centres, enterprises and critical-infrastructure networks. That is the honest boundary of this item — there is no confirmed utility victim and no confirmed OT impact. It earns a place here because of where this hardware tends to live in an electricity network: cheap, capable routers are a common choice for cellular or fixed-wireless backhaul at unmanned substations, distributed generation sites and storage compounds, often installed by a contractor and often the one device on that site with a route to both the corporate network and the RTU.

items.title: Check Point confirms attackers are exploiting the CVSS 9.8 VPN flaw the Dutch NCSC warned about — CISA gives agencies until 25 September
items.content_text: The Netherlands’ National Cyber Security Centre warned on 12 September that exploitation of two Check Point VPN flaws, CVE-2026-85102 and CVE-2026-85103, was imminent. For CVE-2026-85102 that forecast has now been borne out. In an advisory published on 22 September, Check Point says: “Starting September 12, 2026, we observed a wave of exploitation attempts against Spark customers.” The flaw, rated CVSS 9.8, is improper validation of certificate data during VPN negotiation on Security Gateways and Spark firewalls, and it allows unauthenticated remote code execution. Check Point released fixes on 9 September, so exploitation began three days after the patch. CISA added CVE-2026-85102 to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 22 September with a federal remediation deadline of 25 September. Check Point has not given a customer count and has not attributed the activity, but it has published indicators: the certificates used in the attacks carry subjects such as CN=vpn, CN=vpn-user or CN=vpnuser, with OU=users and O=global. The companion flaw, CVE-2026-85103, was not among the 22 September KEV additions. No utility victim has been named. This matters to electricity operators because the Check Point gateway is often the device terminating third-party and vendor access: relay and SCADA vendors, protection contractors, DER aggregators and the remote-engineering paths into substation and generation networks tend to land on the same gateways. The same Check Point advisory also disclosed an exploited management-server flaw, CVE-2026-93616, which has its own card.

items.title: Check Point patches a CVSS 9.8 pre-authentication root flaw in the server that writes your IT/OT boundary policy
items.content_text: Check Point has fixed CVE-2026-91843, a CVSS 9.8 stack overflow in the login process of its Security Management and Log Servers, as reported by The Hacker News on 17 September and SecurityWeek on 18 September from vendor advisory sk1000155. An unauthenticated request carrying an overly long username can lead to remote code execution as root. Multi-Domain Server is also affected; Smart-1 Cloud has already been fixed on the vendor side. Affected on-premises lines include R82.10 up to JHF Take 44, R82 up to Take 126, R81.20 up to Take 166 and R81.10 up to Take 190, plus the end-of-support R81 and R80.x; for R82.20, reporting says no protective hotfix take exists yet across its builds. The Hacker News reports that a Trusted Clients misconfiguration is a precondition — that detail could not be checked against the vendor text, so do not rely on it to rule yourself out. Check Point says it has “no indication” of exploitation in the wild. This is a different flaw from the VPN pair the Dutch NCSC flagged on 12 September, one of which is now exploited, and from CVE-2026-93616, a separate management-server flaw that Check Point disclosed on 22 September as exploited since July (see its card). No exploitation of CVE-2026-91843 itself had been reported as of this edition. It lands on the same estate: at many utilities the Check Point management server is what defines the rules on the firewalls separating corporate IT from generation, substation and control-centre networks, so control of it is control of that boundary.

items.title: A second Check Point management-server flaw was exploited as a zero-day in July — hunt back two months, not just patch
items.content_text: Check Point’s 22 September advisory also disclosed CVE-2026-93616, a CVSS 9.8 flaw in the Security Management web service. It is a pre-authentication path traversal that lets an attacker execute scripts and load Java classes on the server. Check Point says it saw a “handful of pinpointed attacks” exploiting it on 23 July 2026, about two months before a fix became available on 22 September. Reporting lists Security Management Server, Multi-Domain Security Management, Log Server, Multi-Domain Log Server and SmartEvent as affected. CISA added the flaw to KEV on 22 September with a 25 September federal deadline. Targets and actor have not been named. Do not confuse it with CVE-2026-91843, the over-long-username flaw in the same servers, which has its own card and has not been reported exploited. For an electricity operator the management server is the system that writes the rules on the firewalls separating corporate IT from generation, substation and control-centre networks. An attacker who ran code on it in July could have changed those rules without tripping an alarm.

items.title: CISA adds five exploited flaws to KEV, including the remote-support tool your integrator probably uses
items.content_text: CISA added five vulnerabilities affecting JFrog Artifactory, ConnectWise ScreenConnect and MikroTik RouterOS to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 12 September after evidence of active exploitation, setting federal remediation deadlines of 13 September for RouterOS, 14 September for ScreenConnect and 25 September for Artifactory. Reporting indicates the Artifactory flaws were chained to obtain administrator control, establish persistence and install Rust-based backdoors; ScreenConnect exploitation reportedly enabled unauthorised file transfer and execution through active sessions using a malicious VBScript payload; and the RouterOS entry reflects the CERT Polska chain covered separately on this page. For a utility the ScreenConnect entry is the one to read twice. Remote-support and RMM tooling is how integrators, protection contractors and OEM support desks reach engineering workstations and HMIs, and it is frequently installed outside the asset inventory the security team maintains.

items.title: September ICS Patch Tuesday: Siemens ships nine advisories, Schneider four, with a distribution RTU fix in the pile
items.content_text: The 8 September ICS patch round landed heavier than usual for electricity operators. Siemens issued nine advisories, seven of them on the day, with critical findings in the Reyrolle 7SR5 relay family covered separately above, Open Interface Services, Industrial Edge Management and SIMOVE Fleetmanager/SIPLANT, and began rolling out fixes for Linux kernel flaw CVE-2026-31431 at CVSS 7.8 across affected product lines. Schneider Electric published four. The most severe is a critical authentication vulnerability in Modicon M580 and M580 Safety controllers, CVE-2026-3869 at CVSS 9.2. Closer to the grid edge, Schneider also fixed a high-severity issue in PowerLogic T300 — the former Easergy T300 RTU used for MV feeder automation and substation remote terminal duty — alongside EcoStruxure IT Data Center Expert and a medium-severity SCADAPack x70 defect. Aveva disclosed four flaws in the PIMBoards component of Pipeline Integrity Monitor, and CISA published them on 10 September as ICSA-26-253-01: CVE-2026-81821, a hardcoded cryptographic key, and CVE-2026-81822, weak MD5 password hashing, both at CVSS 8.4, alongside a missing-authorisation issue at 5.3 and a cross-site scripting flaw at 4.7, all fixed in Pipeline Integrity Monitor 2025 SP1 P2. Nothing in the round is reported as exploited, and that remained true when the batch was re-checked on 11 September. The T300 item is covered separately below.

items.title: The one genuinely new power item this cycle is a feeder-automation RTU — Schneider’s PowerLogic T300
items.content_text: Schneider Electric’s September 2026 patch release included a high-severity vulnerability in the PowerLogic T300 platform, the rebranded Easergy T300 remote terminal unit used for MV distribution feeder automation and monitoring. It is a separate advisory from the Modicon M580 critical flaw (CVE-2026-3869) and the Siemens Reyrolle 7SR5 relay set published in the same cycle, and it is the only genuinely new electricity-sector disclosure found in the 9–11 September window. Be clear about what is and is not known: the secondary reporting reviewed — SecurityWeek’s ICS Patch Tuesday round-up and the associated conference coverage — characterised the severity only as “high” and did not carry a CVE identifier or a CVSS vector, so none is published here. A vendor fix or mitigation was issued as part of the same September advisory cycle. No exploitation has been reported. The reason it matters out of proportion to a missing score is the device’s job: a T300 sits in a ring main unit or pole-mounted cabinet and actuates switchgear, so it is one of the few products in this month’s pile that can directly change the state of a distribution feeder.

items.title: NIST puts the next edition of SP 800-82, the baseline US guide to OT security, out for comment until 30 November
items.content_text: NIST released the initial public draft of SP 800-82 Revision 4, “Guide to Operational Technology (OT) Security”, on 21 September, with comments due by 30 November 2026. The revision restructures the guide around the NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0 and reorganises the risk-management material to emphasise the CSF Govern function. NIST says it adds guidance on security controls for asset management and network detection, and security architecture principles centred on “protecting system management functions and applying zero trust principles.” Scope expands to building automation, water, food and agriculture, rail, maritime and the Industrial Internet of Things. Industrial Cyber’s review of the 321-page draft, published on 22 September, reports that it calls for a consequence-driven defence mindset, recommends separating OT from enterprise networks and names privileged access management as “the clearest expression of zero trust” in OT. It is guidance, not regulation, and it will not change CIP obligations for registered entities. But auditors, insurers and state regulators commonly cite 800-82, and its emphasis on protecting management functions lines up with this week’s exploited firewall and SD-WAN management systems.

items.title: FERC approves CIP-014-4: one 36-month cycle, jointly owned facilities in scope, and a 1,500-foot look around the fence
items.content_text: FERC has approved NERC reliability standard CIP-014-4, published in the Federal Register on 15 September under section 215 of the Federal Power Act and reported by Industrial Cyber the following day. The standard governs how transmission owners identify and assess the stations and substations whose loss could result in instability, uncontrolled separation or cascading. Four changes matter operationally. Applicability now extends to jointly owned transmission facilities. The previous 30-month and 60-month cycles are consolidated into a single 36-calendar-month review and assessment cycle, aligned with TPL-001 planning. Risk assessments must use steady-state and dynamic simulations across peak and off-peak load cases. And the assessment must consider stations and substations within 1,500 feet, about 457 metres, of the facility in question. The effective date is 1 October 2028, and FERC estimates roughly 344 transmission owners in scope at about ten hours a year each. It follows the 2022 substation attacks and FERC’s December 2022 directive to evaluate CIP-014-3. This is physical security rather than cyber — but the identification step is shared work, because the same station list drives CIP-002 classification, and a facility that changes status under one standard tends to change it under the other.

items.title: CISA makes the case for decoys — and OT is the one place where adding a fake asset is easier than changing a real one
items.content_text: CISA published “Using Cyber Decoys to Strengthen Detection and Response” on 17 September. The guide defines decoys as assets that appear to be legitimate systems, accounts or data but exist to distract adversaries, detect their presence or support the collection of threat intelligence, and it structures deployment across three phases: preparation, execution and analysis. CISA positions the technique alongside zero trust as an incremental, low-disruption detection measure rather than a replacement for controls. It reads better in an OT context than in an IT one for a simple reason: the standard objection to new detection in a control environment is that touching a production system carries risk, and a decoy does not touch one. A fake historian, a spare engineering workstation that is not actually used, or a honeytoken credential seeded on a jump host changes nothing in the process. And because legitimate traffic inside a control network is narrow and predictable, a single interaction with a decoy is a far higher-quality alert than most of what a utility SOC currently spends its day triaging. The cost is maintenance: a decoy that stops matching the estate around it becomes obvious to an attacker and useless to you.

items.title: CISA retires its weekly vulnerability bulletin on 28 September — check whether your patch process quietly depends on it
items.content_text: CISA will stop publishing its weekly Vulnerability Summary bulletin from 28 September, SecurityWeek reported on 17 September, directing users instead to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue, alerts and advisories. The agency frames the change as consistent with Binding Operational Directive 26-04 of June 2026 and its shift towards risk-based prioritisation. Nothing in the reporting indicates that ICS advisories are affected. The practical question for a utility is procedural rather than technical. The weekly summary is a common input to vulnerability-management routines and, in more than a few programmes, it is the documented patch source named in the evidence trail kept for NERC CIP-007 patch-management obligations. If a procedure of yours points at that bulletin, the source needs changing before the end of the month, and the change itself needs recording. KEV and the ICS advisory feed are the obvious replacements, with one caveat worth stating in the procedure: KEV is deliberately narrower, listing only what is known to be exploited, so a programme that swaps one for the other without adjusting its criteria will quietly stop tracking a great deal it used to see.

items.title: ENISA switches on the Single Reporting Platform as the Cyber Resilience Act’s vulnerability reporting duties take effect
items.content_text: The EU Agency for Cybersecurity deployed the initial operating capability of its Single Reporting Platform, announced 14 September, giving manufacturers and open-source software stewards the channel they need to meet Cyber Resilience Act reporting obligations that took effect this month. Under the CRA, makers of products with digital elements must report actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe incidents on a defined clock, with an early warning followed by a fuller notification. For a utility the CRA is mostly a procurement lever rather than a direct obligation: it is your relay, RTU, inverter and gateway vendors who now carry the reporting duty, and their disclosures are about to become more timely and more visible. Reported here factually as a regulatory milestone, without comment on the underlying policy debate.

items.title: DOE names Frenos, Raptor Dynamix and Bastazo under its SENTRY energy cybersecurity programme
items.content_text: The US Department of Energy’s Office of Cybersecurity, Energy Security, and Emergency Response (CESER) announced on 14 September three recipients under its Securing ENergy Technology ResiliencY (SENTRY) programme, which runs through ConnectWerx. Frenos is building AI-driven adversary emulation for energy-sector attack scenarios; Raptor Dynamix is developing a counter-drone system for utilities it calls Grid Guardian; and Bastazo is building a cyber-informed engineering risk-quantification framework. DOE did not publish award amounts. The relevance to an operator is less the awards than what they signal about where federal attention in grid security is going: adversary emulation against energy environments, drones as a physical threat to utility sites, and engineering-led risk quantification. It sits alongside the Department’s request for industry input on bulk-power equipment and supply-chain risk, and is reported here factually, without comment on the policy direction.

items.title: DOE has opened the comment window that decides what grid-equipment provenance will actually mean
items.content_text: The Department of Energy published a Request for Information in the Federal Register on 9 September implementing the executive order of 26 August that declared a national emergency over bulk-power-system security. The RFI asks industry for input on foreign ownership and control, equipment provenance, firmware and software integrity, and remote-access practices for grid-connected equipment, naming inverters, battery energy storage, uninterruptible power supplies, generators and industrial control systems. Comments are due 9 October 2026, and DOE held its public webinar on 16 September. This is the mechanism that turns August’s order into procurement and compliance obligations, which makes a four-week window the only inexpensive opportunity to shape what those obligations look like in practice. The substantive point for an operator is that the questions DOE is asking — who manufactured this, what firmware is on it, and who can reach it remotely — are ones most CIP-013 supply-chain programmes cannot currently answer for inverter-based resources and storage, because that equipment usually arrives through an EPC contract rather than being bought directly.

items.title: EU Cyber Resilience Act reporting went live on 11 September — 24 hours to tell ENISA about an exploited flaw
items.content_text: The vulnerability and incident reporting obligations of the EU Cyber Resilience Act took effect on 11 September 2026. Manufacturers of products with digital elements must now notify an actively exploited vulnerability or a severe security incident through ENISA’s Single Reporting Platform within 24 hours of becoming aware of it, follow up within 72 hours with detail on the exploit and mitigation status, and file a final report within 14 days of a fix becoming available. They must also inform affected users. The regime reaches manufacturers placing products on the EU market regardless of where they are based, with penalties running to €15 million at the top of the scale. For a utility the practical effect is on the supply side rather than the compliance side: relay, RTU, EMS/SCADA, inverter and DER-platform vendors selling into Europe are now on a 24-hour clock, so exploitation-confirmed disclosures about grid equipment should surface faster and in a more standardised form than the sector is used to.

items.title: 117 federal reporting rules across 27 agencies — and the first hours of an incident are when they collide
items.content_text: The McCrary Institute and the US Chamber of Commerce published analysis on 8 September, drawing on Government Accountability Office work, counting 117 separate federal cyber incident reporting regulations spread across 27 agencies, 48 of which apply to private industry. Their argument is operational rather than ideological: duplicative notifications with different thresholds, formats and clocks pull the same small group of people away from containment during the hours when containment is most effective. Electricity operators recognise the shape of this — a single event at a registered entity can trigger E-ISAC reporting, an OE-417 to the Department of Energy, NERC CIP-008 obligations, state utility commission notification, and, for entities with federal contracts or regulated data, more besides. The analysis lands as CIRCIA rules are expected to be finalised this autumn, which is the point at which harmonisation either happens or does not.
